Q: microtime() to seconds or hours or minutes conversion A:

microtime() to seconds or hours or min conversion?

microtime() is the name of the PHP function that return a measure of time in microseconds and basically microseconds can be converted to:

1 milliseconds = 1,000 microseconds
1 second       = 1,000,000 microseconds
1 minute       = 60,000,000 microseconds
1 hour         = 3,600,000,000 microseconds

Or

1 microsecond = 0.001 milliseconds
1 microsecond = 0.000001 seconds
1 microsecond = 0.0000000166666667 minutes
1 microsecond = 0.000000000277777778 hours

Q: CORS Chrome Extension with manifest version 2 A:

Update 2025-03-03: Well Chrome got updated this morning to only allow v3 and all my favorite extensions are dead now, including my ad blocker. So I'm moving on... I'm just going to use a different (chromium-based) browser, but thanks for the upvotes.

Update 2024-07-03: This all applies to "manifest_version": 2 and even though Google has been threatening for a while to reject it, I'm still using it. Mainly because v3 doesn't have .getPackageDirectoryEntry() which means I can't listen to my files and have hot reload. So I'm hoping they'll add that back in (or something similar) before I have to switch.

Prologue

If you're trying to hit an API from your extension, this should be fine. But a site has to allow requests that don't come from its own domain for this to work. (If you're still seeing the error after this, that's why.)

Explanation

As of Chrome 73, cross site requests are blocked. (Even if you have the hosts in your permissions property.) Some sites seem to get through unblocked but I'm sure eventually most won't.

You have to make the request in a background page...

Setup

Add a section to your manifest.json to point to the background page.

"background": {
  "scripts": ["bg_page.js"],
  "persistent": false
}

Create the background page: bg_page.js

chrome.runtime.onMessage.addListener(
    function(url, sender, onSuccess) {
        fetch(url)
            .then(response => response.text())
            .then(responseText => onSuccess(responseText));

        return true; // will respond asynchronously.
    }
);

Then use it in your main.js

chrome.runtime.sendMessage( //goes to bg_page.js
      url,
      data => dataProcessFunction(data) //your callback
);

Additional Tips

If you do anything like console.log() from the bg page, click the "inspect views background page" link in your extension's square in chrome's extensions manager and you'll get a separate dev tools window for everything that happens with your background page.

If you want to see the docs for yourself:

  • https://developer.chrome.com/docs/extensions/mv2/background_pages/
  • https://www.chromium.org/Home/chromium-security/extension-content-script-fetches/#2-avoid-cross-origin-fetches-in-content-scripts

Q: Migrating data to a new database -> On-Prem or Cloud? A:

Start researching by reading about the features and prices of each cloud platform.

Cloud

The main advantage of the cloud is that you don't have to equip your own servers, and then worry about rack space, power and AC, hardware failures, backups, upgrades, capital expense accounting... and that's before you even start thinking about software.

Cloud hosting is attractive because it relieves you of a lot of physical system administration chores.

On the other hand, you'll be surprised at how much system administration you end up having to do in the cloud, like network configuration, load balancing, DNS, and on and on. It's complex enough that your business will probably need a full-time technical staff person with lots of training and experience to manage it.

Another disadvantage of the cloud (for some people) is that you are constrained by the services they offer. If their managed database is configured right for you, that's lucky. But if you outgrow it, or you need any configuration option different than what they offer, then you're kind of stuck.

Finally, a cloud database tends to be more expensive if you run the database 24/7. They have options for databases that scale up and down if you have sporadic usage. You might find ways of being more economical, but that takes a lot of planning and understanding of your usage patterns.

Here are a couple of links about cloud managed databases to get you started, but expect to study dozens of other detailed web pages. The pages below should direct you to them.

  • What is Azure SQL Database?
  • What is Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS)?
  • Google Cloud Databases

You may also contact these companies and work with one of their Solutions Architects (basically a salesperson with some technical knowledge). They'll interview you to understand your needs, then recommend a product to you. But they'll probably try to upsell you to more services than you really need. They are salespeople first.

You should really do both. It will help you to avoid being flim-flammed by the salesperson if you gain some knowledge independently.

On-Premise

Basically, it's DIY time. You get to install and administer all hardware and software. You have the greatest flexibility and control, so it's good for bespoke solutions. You might optimize by using capital accounting, but you'll balance that with your own labor to maintain the servers.

Some people might say that the general trend is for business to abandon their old on-premise datacenters and move to the cloud, but that's not universal. There are some businesses who are even moving operations from the cloud back to a datacenter. Or some who use both cloud and on-premise for different parts of their operations. There's no single right answer for everyone.

Non-Cloud Hosting

You can find monthly domain hosting services besides the big three cloud vendors. This is the cheapest option, and simplest because you have the least options for configuration.

But you also have the least control over the administration, and there might be gaps like backups don't happen reliably, or the version of database software lags behind the current version (sometimes by a lot). You might have other headaches, like suffering with "noisy neighbors" — other customers of the hosting company who overload a shared database server and make your database slow at unpredictable times.

To find one of these services, run a Google search for "best domain hosting in 2025" (or whatever year), and read the reviews. As with any internet reviews, take them with a grain of salt. The only way to really find the best one for you is to try them out yourself.

  • 9 Best Domain Hosting Services (2026)
  • The Best Web Hosting Services for 2026 (PCMag)
  • Best web hosting services (ZDNet)

The Bottom Line

There's not really a "best practice" that fits all needs. Any of these could be the right balance of features, convenience, and price for you.
